Cautionary Statement Regarding Forward-Looking Statements

nodes.title: Walmart Business, History, and Segments
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its omnichannel retail strategy, global customer and store footprint, everyday-low-price and cost disciplines, three reporting segments, fiscal year, 2026 revenue, headquarters, and stock listing. It traces the company’s development from its founders’ variety stores through discount stores, clubs, supercenters, international expansion, eCommerce, acquisitions, and investments in technology, AI, supply chains, and services. It also outlines its global retail, wholesale, and eCommerce operations and notes segment contributions and related financial-statement disclosures.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment Overview
nodes.summary: Walmart U.S., the company’s largest segment, operates 4,611 stores across the U.S. and Puerto Rico, Walmart.com, and its app; it reported $483.0 billion in fiscal 2026 sales. Its omnichannel services integrate stores and eCommerce through pickup, delivery, in-home delivery, digital pharmacy, and Walmart+ benefits. Merchandise spans grocery, general merchandise, and health and wellness; category presentations may be revised for comparability. The segment sells national, private-label, and licensed brands and also offers advertising, marketplace fulfillment, supplier analytics, fuel, and financial services.

nodes.title: Walmart International Segment
nodes.summary: Walmart International operates 5,743 stores across 18 countries through wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries, using retail, wholesale, club, cash-and-carry and eCommerce formats. Fiscal 2026 sales were $130.4 billion (19% of consolidated sales), up from $121.9 billion in 2025 and $114.6 billion in 2024. Its strategy emphasizes affordable products and services, local expertise, sustainable growth, omnichannel shopping, pickup and delivery, marketplaces, advertising, private and local brands, supplier relationships, financial services and healthcare. Sam’s Club U.S. operates 601 membership-only clubs in 44 states and Puerto Rico, plus digital channels; fiscal 2026 sales were $93.0 billion (13% of consolidated sales), versus $90.2 billion in 2025 and $86.2 billion in 2024, with membership income significant to operating income. Annual Club and Plus memberships cost $50 and $110, respectively, and include household cards, optional add-ons, tiered benefits and Sam’s Cash rewards. Omnichannel services include pickup, delivery, Scan & Go and Just Go. Merchandise covers grocery and consumables, general merchandise, health and wellness, fuel and other categories; category revisions are applied to prior-period presentations for comparability. Member’s Mark offers value-priced premium products, and other services include advertising, supplier analytics, installation, photo and tech assistance, home and auto solutions, and financial products.

nodes.title: Walmart International and Sam’s Club U.S.
nodes.summary: Covers Walmart International’s integrated store and eCommerce services, marketplace expansion, merchandise and private brands, local suppliers, and complementary businesses. Describes Sam’s Club U.S.’s locations, sales, membership-based model, membership tiers and benefits, omnichannel services, four merchandise categories and their products, reporting-category revisions, Member’s Mark brand, and additional advertising, supplier, installation, technical, home, auto, and financial offerings.

nodes.title: Competition, Seasonality, and Supply Chain
nodes.summary: The page describes intense, evolving competition across physical, online, and omnichannel retail and related services, the factors shaping competitive position, and strategies including EDLP, cost control, omnichannel services, business expansion, store investment, and technology, automation, AI, and associate development. Sales vary by country, holidays, customs, and weather, with the fourth quarter historically strongest. It outlines global supplier relationships and standards, supply-chain factors affecting product availability and assortment, ongoing automation and fulfillment investments, distribution networks and shipping methods, and the fiscal 2026 integration of Sam’s Club U.S. supply-chain operations with Walmart U.S.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property, Shared Value and Workforce
nodes.summary: The page describes Walmart’s intellectual property protections, registrations, patent applications and licensing, and its exposure to varied U.S. and international laws and regulations. It outlines shared-value priorities—opportunity, sustainability, community, and ethics and integrity—and related stakeholder commitments and ESG reporting. It also summarizes workforce size and composition, alongside a strategy to develop talent, align skills and technology with business needs, enable AI and digital tools, redesign work, and maintain fair, competitive, performance-based practices.

nodes.title: Risk Factors and Omnichannel Strategy
key_items: Failure to successfully execute our omnichannel strategy and the cost of our investments in eCommerce and technology may materially adversely affect our market position, net sales and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company cautions that disclosed risks are not exhaustive or fully predictable and could harm its business, results, finances, liquidity, or securities. It describes the rapid shift to digital retail and risks that investments in omnichannel capabilities—including eCommerce, technology, AI, talent, automation, advertising, acquisitions, partnerships, and store initiatives—may fail to sustain growth or market position. Poor execution, changing customer perceptions, asset impairments, and online sales diverting traffic from stores could reduce sales; investment costs and operating losses may hurt near-term results, while unrealized benefits could damage long-term performance.

nodes.title: If we do not timely identify or effectively respond to consumer trends or preferences, it could negatively affect our reputation, relationship with our customers, demand for the products and services we sell, our market share and the growth of our business.
nodes.summary: Failure to anticipate consumer trends, demand, and shopping patterns can damage reputation, customer relationships, sales, market share, and growth. Forecasting depends on relevant data, merchandise selection, inventory, pricing, promotions, and effective fulfillment; mistakes can cause lost sales, spoilage, markdowns, shortages, excess stock, disruptions, and higher costs. Customers increasingly value price transparency, assortment, experience, convenience, and shipping, requiring investment in digital and AI tools. Negative publicity or incidents—including theft, flawed or biased AI, and data breaches involving the company or partners—can erode trust and trigger boycotts, unrest, investigations, or other harm. Changing and contested social and environmental expectations create reputational risks, affecting sales, relationships, and workforce recruitment and retention. Growing fulfillment-network complexity may make effective operations difficult, with no assurance of success.

nodes.title: We face strong competition from other retailers, wholesale club operators, omnichannel retailers and other businesses which could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company faces intense, evolving competition across physical, eCommerce and omnichannel retail and related services, including from new entrants and AI-powered shopping tools. Competition spans price, selection, service, convenience, digital experience, data and delivery; failure to adapt or execute strategy could harm financial performance. Intellectual-property protections may be unavailable or ineffective, allowing infringement or equivalent innovations. Industry consolidation, alliances, and reduced operations may strengthen competitors’ resources, access, reach and offerings, further threatening performance.

nodes.title: General or macro-economic factors, both domestically and internationally, may materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to financial performance from domestic and international economic conditions, including inflation, interest rates, energy and other costs, employment, consumer spending and credit, currency, taxes, regulation, trade barriers, and recession. These may weaken demand, shift sales toward lower-margin goods, raise expenses, disrupt suppliers, slow inventory turnover, require markdowns, and cause asset impairments. Strategic alliances may underperform or harm competitiveness. Pandemics can disrupt demand, inventory, supply chains, costs, staffing, and other risk areas. Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical conflict, violence, and similar events may damage or close facilities, limit operations, and create workforce and transportation challenges.

nodes.title: Economic, Alliance, and Health Crisis Risks
key_items: The performance of strategic alliances and other business relationships to support the expansion of our business could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
Global or regional health pandemics or epidemics could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: Economic changes—including shifts in consumer credit, spending, taxes, regulation, trade, and costs—may reduce demand and margins, increase expenses and inventory markdowns, impair assets, and affect suppliers’ costs or availability. Strategic alliances may underperform expectations, harm competitiveness, or adversely affect financial results. Pandemics and other health crises can disrupt demand, operations, inventory, supply chains, costs, and financial performance, while intensifying risks involving consumer behavior, competition, reputation, technology, labor, litigation, and regulation.

nodes.title: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, catastrophic and other events could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to financial performance from natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical violence and other disruptions, which can damage facilities, interrupt operations, staffing, customer access, digital services, supply chains and infrastructure, raise costs, and cause losses; U.S.-concentrated impacts may be especially significant. Supplier risks include instability, financial or compliance failures, labor and material shortages, weather, quality, transport, currency, inflation and trade restrictions. Product quality or safety failures may trigger recalls, customer loss, injury claims, and reputational or financial harm, particularly where suppliers cannot indemnify the company.

nodes.title: Supplier, Product, and Operational Risks
key_items: Risks associated with our suppliers could materially adversely affect our financial performance.

If the quality or safety of products we sell in stores or online fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could lose customers, incur liability for any injuries caused by a product we sell or otherwise experience a material impact to our brand, reputation and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text describes how severe events can disrupt U.S. and other operations, supply chains, infrastructure, customer access, and demand, while causing physical losses and higher costs that may harm financial performance. Supplier risks include instability, noncompliance, capacity, labor, materials, weather, transport, currency, inflation, and trade restrictions. Product quality or safety failures may trigger recalls, customer losses, injury claims, and reputational and financial damage, particularly when suppliers cannot meet indemnification obligations.

nodes.title: Marketplace Product and Information-System Risks
key_items: If the quality or safety of products offered for sale on our third-party marketplace fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could be held directly liable, lose customers, become subject to regulatory enforcement or otherwise experience reputational harm.

We rely extensively on information and financial systems to process transactions, summarize results and manage our business. Disruptions in our systems could harm our ability to conduct our operations.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from third-party marketplace products, including unsettled retailer liability, complex seller arrangements, unsafe, noncompliant, counterfeit or infringing goods, enforcement limits, customer and reputational harm, and adverse business effects. It also covers reliance on information and financial systems, threats and outages that could disrupt operations or compromise data, incomplete redundancy and recovery planning, costly repairs and security, and increased disruption risk or missed benefits from technology upgrades and integration.

nodes.title: If the technology-based systems that give our customers the ability to shop with us online and enable us to deliver products and services do not function effectively, or keep pace with similar offerings of our competitors, our operating results, as well as our ability to grow our omnichannel business globally, could be materially adversely affected.
nodes.summary: The company’s global omnichannel growth and results depend on effective, competitive technology and digital platforms. It uses websites, apps, social media, emerging agentic platforms, and digital communications for shopping and customer engagement, and offers store and club pickup, delivery, and shipping. It invests in automation and AI to improve customer and associate experiences and business operations, but must keep pace with changing expectations and competitors while preserving direct customer relationships. AI adoption carries uncertain benefits and operational, legal, privacy, regulatory, litigation, and reputational risks. Failures in company or third-party systems, including cybersecurity incidents, could disrupt service; inadequate, insecure, costly, or outdated digital offerings could weaken competitiveness, sales, reputation, eCommerce growth, and overall results.

nodes.title: Any failure to maintain the privacy or security of the information relating to our company, customers, members, associates, business partners and vendors, whether as a result of cyberattacks on our information systems or otherwise, could damage our reputation, result in litigation or other legal actions against us, result in fines, penalties, and liability, cause us to incur substantial additional costs and materially adversely affect our business and operating results.
nodes.summary: The text describes the company’s extensive cybersecurity and privacy risks: it processes customer, member, employee, vendor, payment, consumer, and protected health data, including through third parties and digital platforms. Evolving attacks—such as ransomware, phishing, AI-enabled intrusion and identity fraud—may exploit human, technical, legacy, remote-work, or vendor vulnerabilities; detection and investigation can be difficult, and incidents have occurred, including in fiscal 2026. Breaches or system disruptions could impair operations, eCommerce, supply chains, and payments; cause data misuse, sales losses, reputational harm, litigation, remediation costs, regulatory penalties, and material financial damage, including cascading effects on partners. Controls cannot eliminate risk, insurance may not cover losses, and payment-card standards, privacy laws, breach-notification duties, HIPAA, and evolving AI and consumer-protection rules impose further obligations and liabilities.

nodes.title: Changes in third-party reimbursements and contracts, type, or scope of offerings of our health and wellness business could adversely affect our overall results of operations, cash flows and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from pharmacy reimbursement, payer and formulary changes, drug costs and availability, competition, regulation, and health-service demand that could harm sales, margins, cash flow, and liquidity; supplier disruptions could also drive customers away. It describes labor-market, wage, benefits, legal, and leadership risks, plus misconduct, fraud, or harm caused by contractors and service providers. Financial risks include missing market expectations and stock-price volatility, and adverse effects from translating foreign operations into U.S. dollars amid exchange-rate fluctuations.

nodes.title: Operational, Labor, Contractor, and Financial Risks
key_items: Our failure to attract and retain qualified associates, increases in wage and benefit costs, changes in laws and other labor issues could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
Illegal or inappropriate activity of our independent contractors or third-party service providers could expose us to liability and adversely affect our business, reputation and financial performance.
Failure to meet market expectations for our financial performance could adversely affect the market price and volatility of our stock.
nodes.summary: Pharmaceutical supply disruptions could damage reputation, shift customers, and reduce sales, margins, service reimbursement, cash flow, and liquidity. Labor shortages, rising wages and benefits, legal changes, competition for talent, and leadership transitions could impair service and financial results. Contractor or provider misconduct, fraud, injury, or damage may trigger reputational, regulatory, litigation, and business harms. Missing financial expectations or changes in growth, spending, dividends, taxes, estimates, or peer performance could lower stock price and increase volatility.

nodes.title: Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may materially adversely affect our financial performance and our reported results of operations.
nodes.summary: Foreign-exchange fluctuations can materially harm reported results. Because international operations use local currencies while consolidated statements are in U.S. dollars, translating financial results at changing rates can cause adverse period-over-period changes, affecting Walmart International and consolidated performance. Currency movements can also raise costs for products purchased in a currency different from the selling country’s currency; if prices cannot or will not be increased, gross profit declines. Unfavorable fluctuations have harmed results and may continue to do so.

nodes.title: Legal, Tax, Regulatory, Compliance, Reputational and Other Risks
nodes.summary: Walmart’s international retail and eCommerce operations, which generated about 19% of fiscal 2026 consolidated sales, face risks that could harm business, financial performance, and reputation. These include political and economic instability; changing trade rules, sanctions, conflicts, and consumer boycotts; regulatory, competition, product-safety, environmental, tax, labor, anti-money-laundering, currency, consumer, and data-protection requirements; inflation and devaluation; and challenges managing operations across jurisdictions, including tax and intellectual-property enforcement. Government actions and geopolitical uncertainty may disrupt operations and consumer confidence. Associates, contractors, or agents may also violate applicable anti-corruption or sanctions laws despite company policies and compliance programs.

nodes.title: Our international operations subject us to legislative, judicial, accounting, legal, regulatory, tax, political and economic risks and conditions specific to the countries or regions in which we operate, which could materially adversely affect our business or financial performance.
nodes.summary: Unfavorable currency movements can reduce Walmart International and consolidated reported performance, raise costs for goods bought in foreign currencies, and erode gross profit when prices cannot be adjusted. International operations, which generated about 19% of fiscal 2026 net sales, face broad political, economic, legal, tax, regulatory, trade, currency, labor, data-protection, competition, safety, and environmental risks across their markets and supply chains. Restrictions, sanctions, conflicts, inflation, devaluation, consumer boycotts, cultural and jurisdictional differences, operational complexity, tax issues, and weaker intellectual-property enforcement may disrupt business, harm financial results or reputation, and be difficult to mitigate. Associates, contractors, or agents may also violate anti-bribery, sanctions, or other laws despite company policies and compliance programs, exposing Walmart to penalties and reputational or financial harm.

nodes.title: Changes in tax and trade laws, regulations and interpretations could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart warns that shifting U.S. and international tax and trade laws, tariffs, restrictions, and interpretations could materially harm financial performance. U.S. segments generate about 82% of sales, and imported merchandise makes the company vulnerable to higher purchasing, selling, and strategic-initiative costs; tariff effects occurred in fiscal 2026 and uncertainty continues into 2027. Tax risks include estimation uncertainty, changing laws, rates, transfer pricing, reporting obligations, the Tax Act, and evolving OECD Pillar Two rules, potentially raising taxes, compliance costs, and audit disputes. Tax-authority reviews may ultimately produce liabilities differing materially from recorded estimates, affecting earnings and cash flows.

nodes.title: Changes in and/or failure to comply with other laws, regulations and interpretations of such laws and regulations specific to the businesses and jurisdictions in which we operate could materially adversely affect our reputation, market position or our business and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text warns that evolving laws, interpretations, enforcement, scrutiny, and failure to comply across jurisdictions may damage reputation, operations, and financial results. It covers extensive healthcare and pharmacy rules; controlled substances, pricing, reimbursement, fraud, and health reform; financial services and fintech regulation; and broad requirements involving competition, safety, environment, consumer protection, sanctions, labor, data, AI, and reporting. It details changing privacy and cybersecurity regimes and compliance costs, China data-transfer approvals, marketing restrictions, VIZIO’s FTC order through 2037, and potential investigations, fines, litigation, license or program exclusions, contract losses, operational changes, and other penalties.

nodes.title: Litigation Risks and Shareholder Forum Provisions
key_items: We are subject to risks related to litigation claims, and other legal proceedings that may materially adversely affect our results of operations, financial position and liquidity.

Our amended and restated bylaws designate the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware as the sole and exclusive forum for certain types of actions and proceedings that may be initiated by our shareholders, which could increase the costs for our shareholders to bring claims, discourage our shareholders from bringing claims, or limit our shareholders' ability to obtain a favorable judicial forum for disputes with us or our directors, officers, associates or shareholders in such capacity.
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive global litigation, investigations and claims involving products, employment, competition, consumer protection, pricing, and other matters, which may be costly, prolonged, and materially harm its business and financial results. It discusses self-insured liabilities, insurance limitations, property-loss exposure, and references further case disclosures. Bylaws make Delaware’s Court of Chancery the exclusive forum for certain shareholder claims, potentially raising costs or restricting forum choice; federal securities-law jurisdiction remains unaffected.

nodes.title: Social and Environmental Risks and Cybersecurity Oversight
key_items: Not satisfying stakeholder expectations with respect to our social and environmental efforts could adversely affect our reputation or subject us to regulatory or litigation risk.
Board of Directors' oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats
Management's role in assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
nodes.summary: The page warns that failing to meet evolving stakeholder expectations for social and environmental goals may harm reputation, morale, customer or shareholder support, or prompt regulatory challenges and litigation; goals and initiatives are not guaranteed. It reports no unresolved staff comments. It describes Walmart’s cybersecurity approach and trust commitments, the Board’s delegation of oversight to the Audit Committee and its reporting processes, and management’s program, incident response and escalation practices, including the CISO’s and CTO’s relevant experience.

nodes.title: Risk Management and Strategy
nodes.summary: Walmart’s cybersecurity program follows frameworks such as NIST-CSF and evolves with laws and standards. It uses layered safeguards and dedicated experts, collaborating with industry groups and third parties. Key practices include risk-based security and privacy reviews, threat monitoring and control updates; incident response and recovery plans; third-party risk management; recurring training; and periodic assessments, testing, and external reviews. Systems and providers have faced incidents and threats, but none are currently known to have materially affected or likely materially affect Walmart. Future material incidents remain possible; further risks appear in Item 1A.

Introduces Walmart’s forward-looking-statement cautions, company history, business model, reporting segments, sales, operations, memberships, products, services, competition, seasonality, supply chain, intellectual property, social and sustainability priorities, workforce, associate development, executive officers, and SEC information. It details risks involving strategy and consumer trends; competition, economic conditions, crises, suppliers, products, marketplaces, technology, cybersecurity, health services, labor, currencies, international operations, taxes, trade, regulation, litigation, and social and environmental expectations. It also describes cybersecurity governance, risk management, controls, and incident response.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity Risk Management and Strategy
key_items: Protecting our technology and information systems
nodes.summary: The cybersecurity program draws on industry frameworks such as NIST-CSF, adapts to legal and standards changes, and uses layered safeguards and dedicated teams, with support from external partners. It assesses and protects technology through impact reviews, monitoring, threat research, and evolving controls; maintains incident response and recovery plans covering severity, escalation, reporting, and mitigation; manages risks from third-party systems and users; and provides recurring, risk- and role-based security training.

nodes.title: Assessments and testing
key_items: I. SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION; II. ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: Walmart periodically tests cybersecurity policies through exercises, threat modeling, vulnerability assessments, and third parties, updating controls as needed. It reports incidents but no known material effects or likely material risks, while acknowledging future risk. The text details retail-unit counts and square footage, owned and leased stores and distribution facilities, office and lease arrangements, and property reporting dates. It also lists significant opioid, DOJ, False Claims Act, ASDA equal-value, driver-platform, Mexico and India antitrust proceedings; notes $3.3 billion in opioid settlements paid; and describes an EPA Clean Air Act refrigeration-program investigation with possible penalties over $1 million and an uncertain outcome.

title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

nodes.title: Recent Developments, Macroeconomic Conditions and Potential Impacts
nodes.summary: This MD&A reviews fiscal 2026, 2025, and 2024 results, explaining financial statement changes, performance metrics, and the contributions of three business segments. It describes segment operating income measures and how currency impacts are calculated, including the exclusion of non-USD acquisitions during their first 12 months. It outlines economic uncertainties—tariffs, inflation, currencies, consumer confidence, employment, fuel, and supply chains—and the company’s pricing, sourcing, and merchandising responses. It also notes that the 2025 OBBB Act’s tax effects were immaterial to tax expense and effective rate, though certain provisions reduced fiscal 2026 cash taxes and may shift future payments.

nodes.title: Company Performance Metrics
nodes.summary: The company’s priorities are growth, margin improvement and returns through disciplined investment. Growth focuses on omnichannel shopping, comparable sales, membership and eCommerce. The text defines comparable sales and its calculation limitations, then reports fiscal 2026/2025 results: Walmart U.S. rose 4.3%/4.8%, driven by tickets, transactions and broad category strength, with eCommerce contributions of 4.3%/2.9%; Sam’s Club U.S. rose 2.9%/4.7%, with eCommerce contributions of 3.3%/2.3%, partly offset by fuel impacts of 1.9%/1.5%. Margin strategy emphasizes productivity, cost control, business mix and operating-income leverage. Company net sales were $706.4 billion in 2026 versus $674.5 billion in 2025; gross profit rates rose 8/40 basis points, while expense rates increased 20/36 basis points. The text explains the drivers, including inventory management, higher-margin growth, mix shifts, claims costs, compensation changes, depreciation, variable pay and marketing. Operating-income margin fell 13 basis points in 2026 and rose 15 in 2025, reflecting these factors and membership-income growth.

nodes.title: Returns
key_items: Return on Assets and Return on Investment
nodes.summary: Walmart expects returns on capital to improve through its financial framework and provides shareholder returns via repurchases and dividends. It uses GAAP return on assets (ROA) and non-GAAP return on investment (ROI), explaining their formulas, ROI’s usefulness and comparability limits, and reconciling ROI to ROA with fiscal 2026 and 2025 financial data. ROA rose from 7.9% to 8.2%, mainly due to higher net income, partly offset by asset growth. ROI fell from 15.5% to 15.1% as invested capital increased; improved operating income partly offset share-based compensation, legal, and restructuring charges.

nodes.title: Capital Allocation
nodes.summary: Walmart prioritizes capital spending on higher-return automation and omnichannel areas, including eCommerce, supply chain, technology, customer-facing initiatives, and store/club remodels, new locations, and expansions; tables show allocations and total expenditures for fiscal 2025–2026. The text defines free cash flow (operating cash flow less property-and-equipment payments), explains its non-GAAP, supplemental limits and comparability, and reconciles it with GAAP operating cash flow and investing/financing cash flows for fiscal 2024–2026. It attributes fiscal 2026 operating cash flow and free cash flow growth to operating income, lower taxes, and payment timing, partly offset by higher capital spending; fiscal 2025 results reflect operating income, prior-year opioid-charge payments, inventory purchases, and increased capital expenditures.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Reports consolidated and segment results for fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024, including sales, revenue, income, margins, stores and square footage. Consolidated revenue and net income rose in 2026 and 2025, driven mainly by comparable sales, eCommerce and membership growth; results also reflect foreign-exchange impacts, changing gross margins, higher operating expenses, investment valuation gains or losses, taxes and EPS. Walmart U.S. sales and operating income increased, with growth from transactions, tickets, membership and omnichannel sales. Walmart International sales grew, but 2026 operating income fell amid currency effects, mix shifts and PhonePe-related charges. Sam’s Club sales and income increased, supported by membership and comparable sales, with fuel-price effects, margin changes, fulfillment costs and higher expenses discussed. Definitions and the rationale for excluding fuel from Sam’s results are provided.

It details dividends and payment dates, repurchase authorizations, activity and funding approach, material operating and contractual cash requirements, purchase obligations, capital resources and debt ratings, including factors and risks affecting ratings and market access.

nodes.title: Summary of Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP financial reporting relies on management estimates and judgments based on past events and expected outcomes; actual results may differ, and policies are continually reviewed. For contingencies, liabilities are accrued when losses are probable and estimable, material reasonably possible losses are disclosed, and matters are reviewed quarterly; unresolved cases could materially affect the company. Uncertain tax benefits are recognized when more likely than not to withstand tax-authority challenge, reassessed as circumstances change, and require judgment and interpretation of complex tax laws.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The text defines internal control over financial reporting, its objectives and inherent limitations, and includes Ernst & Young’s signed report dated March 13, 2026. nodes.title: Note 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Walmart Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its omnichannel retail business and three reportable segments. Its consolidated statements include subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany items, consolidate qualifying variable-interest entities, and use the equity method for significant-influence investments; international operations generally use a one-month reporting lag. GAAP statements rely on estimates that may differ from actual results. Foreign operations’ assets and liabilities use period-end exchange rates, income uses average rates, and translation adjustments enter accumulated other comprehensive loss. Cash equivalents include investments with maturities of three months or less and quickly processed payment transactions; the disclosures also cover cash balances, foreign-held funds, liquidity arrangements, and amounts restricted from transfer to the U.S.

nodes.title: Receivables, Inventory, Property, and Leases
nodes.summary: Receivables are reported net of credit-loss reserves and arise mainly from customer, supplier, tax, and real-estate transactions; customer receivables were $4.9 billion in 2026 versus $4.4 billion in 2025. Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and market or net realizable value, using segment-specific retail or weighted-average methods and LIFO or FIFO; LIFO estimates are adjusted quarterly and reconciled at year-end. Property and equipment are recorded at cost, with improvements capitalized and routine maintenance expensed; the page presents balances, useful lives, depreciation practices, and related expenses. Lease accounting covers identification, discounted ROU assets and obligations, term and discount-rate assumptions, short-term lease exemption, and combining lease and non-lease components.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Goodwill, and Fair Value

nodes.summary: Long-lived assets are tested for recoverability when indicators arise, using store- or club-level cash flows; any impairment is measured at fair value. Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually and as indicated, while definite-lived intangibles are amortized straight-line. The text describes goodwill testing methods, reports no goodwill or significant intangible impairment in fiscal 2024–2026, and provides goodwill balances and activity by segment, including VIZIO-related goodwill. It defines fair value for assets and liabilities and explains recurring fair-value measurement and income recognition for certain equity investments.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies and balances for long-lived asset impairment, goodwill and acquired intangible assets, fair-value measurement, investments, divestiture indemnifications, supplier-financing obligations, and self-insurance. Impairment testing uses store/club cash flows and fair value; goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually and when warranted, while definite-lived intangibles are amortized. It reports goodwill movements by segment, no material impairment charges, and indefinite-lived intangible balances. It also explains investment valuation and Asda debt holdings, indemnity liabilities and maximum exposure, supplier-program terms, balances and cash-flow classification, and actuarial estimation and insurance mitigation of self-insurance reserves.

nodes.title: Debt Investments, Indemnities and Supplier Financing
nodes.summary: Debt investments are carried at cost with observable price or impairment adjustments, or at fair value for trading securities. They are immaterial and mainly comprise the retained Asda investment, valued using Level 3 discounted cash flows and mostly redeemable in fiscal 2029. Divestiture indemnification liabilities were $0.7 billion in 2026 and $0.6 billion in 2025, with maximum potential payments of $3.4 billion. Supplier financing is optional for suppliers, generally has 30–90-day payment terms, and creates no direct financial relationship or economic interest for the Company; the Company pays confirmed invoices on their due dates. Obligations rose from $5.725 billion to $5.989 billion in 2026, are generally accounts payable, and related cash flows are operating activities.

It describes derivative hedging purposes, counterparty credit controls, netting and collateral, accounting treatment, balance-sheet classification, and fair-value interest-rate and cash-flow cross-currency hedges and maturities. It also outlines income-tax accounting, deferred-tax measurement and valuation allowances, effective-rate and discrete-event provisions, and liabilities, interest, and penalties for uncertain tax positions.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies, Pronouncements, and Earnings Per Share

It also covers relevant balances, risks and estimation methods; new accounting standards and their adoption or expected effects; segment cost comparability; and basic and diluted earnings-per-share calculations and reconciliations.

nodes.title: Note 3. Shareholders' Equity
nodes.summary: Note 3 covers Walmart’s equity and compensation. nodes.title: Note 4. Accrued Liabilities
nodes.summary: Note 4 reports accrued liabilities as of January 31, 2026 and 2025, totaling $31.187 billion and $29.345 billion, respectively. Categories are accrued wages and benefits, self-insurance, non-income taxes, deferred gift card revenue, and other liabilities. Notes explain that these cover compensation and benefits; insurance-related claims and healthcare; payroll, property, value-added, sales, and other taxes; and items such as deferred membership revenue, interest, supply chain, advertising, maintenance, and utilities.

nodes.title: Note 5. Short-term Borrowings and Long-term Debt
nodes.summary: Note 5 details short-term borrowings, credit facilities, long-term debt, maturities, issuances, and repayments. nodes.title: Net Operating Losses, Tax Credit Carryforwards and Valuation Allowances
nodes.summary: As of January 31, 2026, the Company had about $19.6 billion in net operating and capital loss carryforwards; $13.1 billion expire in years through 2046, while the remainder do not expire. Deferred tax asset recoverability is assessed using expected taxable income from carrybacks, temporary-difference reversals, operating forecasts, and tax strategies. A valuation allowance is established when recovery is not more likely than not, and later changes are recognized in income. Allowances, primarily for net operating losses, were $4.4 billion in 2026 and $7.4 billion in 2025.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: Tax benefits for uncertain positions are recognized only when more likely than not to withstand tax-authority challenge. Gross unrecognized benefits from continuing operations were $2.4 billion at January 31, 2026, versus $3.8 billion in 2025; $2.0 billion would affect the effective tax rate in both years. A reconciliation for fiscal 2024–2026 reports beginning balances and changes from prior- and current-year positions, settlements, and statute expirations. Related interest and penalties were immaterial. Examinations remain possible for U.S. federal years 2018–2025, international years 2015–2025, and state/local years 2018–2025; generally, earlier years are closed, with few exceptions.

nodes.title: Other Taxes
nodes.summary: The Company faces examinations in various jurisdictions for VAT, sales-based, payroll, and other non-income taxes; some have resulted in assessments or judgments. Individual potential losses are generally immaterial, but adverse outcomes across related matters could create a material liability to the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Note 10. Retirement-Related Benefits
nodes.summary: The Company provides a U.S. 401(k) plan with contributions available upon hire and a Puerto Rico 401(k)-type plan, generally available after one year. After one year, it matches 100% of contributions up to 6% of eligible earnings; matches vest immediately. Participants may contribute up to 50% of pretax earnings, subject to legal limits. Non-U.S. associates abroad participate in locally administered defined contribution arrangements. A table is identified as summarizing U.S., international, and total contribution expense for fiscal 2026, 2025, and 2024, in millions; no figures are shown.

nodes.title: Note 11. Segments and Disaggregated Revenue
nodes.summary: The note describes Walmart’s three reportable segments—Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam’s Club U.S.—their activities, CODM oversight, operating-income performance measure, and limitations on segment comparability; Corporate and support is also reported. It presents fiscal 2024–2026 segment and consolidated revenues, costs, operating income, pretax-income reconciliation, assets, depreciation and capital expenditures, plus U.S./non-U.S. revenue and long-lived assets. It notes fuel expenses, corporate-campus income, no material individual foreign country or customer, and disaggregates segment net sales by merchandise category or market and eCommerce, including definitions and reclassification policy.

nodes.title: The Indentures
nodes.summary: The Notes are governed by three indentures: the 2005, 2002, and 1991 indentures, including their specified amendments and incorporated filing exhibits; Notes issued under each are named accordingly. BNYM serves as trustee under all three, has existing commercial and custodial relationships with the Company, and may provide further banking, trustee, or paying-agent services. The 2005 Indenture is governed by New York law, permits unlimited debt issuance in series, and allows additional substantially identical securities to be issued without existing holders’ consent and consolidated into the same series. Its covenants are limited.

nodes.summary: The text identifies the 2005, 2002 and 1991 indentures, their trustees, amendments and incorporated filing exhibits, and names the notes issued under each. The 2005 Indenture is governed by New York law, allows unlimited debt issuance and additional similar notes to be consolidated into existing series without holder consent. Its limited covenants do not cap debt or leases, restrict secured debt, or limit dividends, distributions, or stock repurchases and redemptions.

nodes.title: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The 2005 Indenture permits the Company to amalgamate, consolidate, merge, reorganize, arrange, or transfer substantially all its assets if the successor assumes the Company’s obligations, is organized under U.S. law, no continuing event of default results, and other indenture conditions are met. The successor then assumes the Company’s rights and powers under the Indenture. A transaction meeting these conditions is not a default or event of default permitting noteholders or the trustee to take related action.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The 2005 Indenture defines series-specific defaults: overdue interest unpaid for 30 days, unpaid principal or premium, covenant or warranty breaches uncured 90 days after written notice, bankruptcy/insolvency/reorganization, and other series-designated events. A default on one series need not affect others. For non-bankruptcy defaults, the trustee or holders of 25% may accelerate that series; bankruptcy defaults automatically accelerate all series. A majority may rescind acceleration if required deposits are made and other defaults are cured or waived. The issuer must annually report defaults. Individual holders may bring proceedings only after specified notice, 25% holder request, indemnity, trustee inaction for 60 days, and no contrary majority direction; remedies benefit holders equally. A series majority may direct trustee remedies and waive certain defaults, subject to limits. The trustee must act with prudent-person care during continuing defaults. Individual holders retain an unimpaired right to sue for payments due.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: The 2005 Indenture generally permits amendments with majority-holder consent, but requires each affected holder’s consent for specified changes to payment terms, enforcement rights, voting thresholds, or amendment provisions. It also lists changes the issuer and trustee may make without holder consent. Majority holders may waive certain defaults or acceleration subject to payment, cure, and other conditions; the trustee may act to protect holders after a continuing default. The 2002 Indenture is governed by New York law, has no debt issuance limit, permits additional same-series securities without consent, and allows securities to be convertible or exchangeable under terms including price or ratio and conversion period.

Identifies the 2005, 2002 and 1991 indentures, their trustees, amendments, incorporated exhibits and notes, and BNYM’s related banking and debt-service roles. The 2005 Indenture is governed by New York law, permits unlimited debt and additional same-series notes without consent, and imposes few financial restrictions. It sets conditions for mergers and asset transfers; defines defaults, acceleration, rescission, trustee duties, holder remedies and annual reporting; and governs amendments and waivers, requiring affected-holder consent for specified fundamental changes. The 2002 Indenture also permits unlimited issuance and same-series additions, and allows convertible or exchangeable securities.

A valid waiver cures the default and resulting event of default. The 2002 Indenture, governed by New York law, permits unlimited debt issuance and additional notes ranking equally and joining an existing series without holder consent. Its debt securities may be convertible or exchangeable, with terms covering prices or ratios, periods, conversion rights, adjustment events, and effects of redemption.

nodes.title: Events of Default and Waiver

A default on one series need not affect others. The trustee or holders of 25% may accelerate; holders of a majority may rescind acceleration or waive eligible defaults, subject to conditions and exceptions. It also describes trustee enforcement duties and indemnity, holders’ individual rights to sue for overdue payments, trustee notice requirements and exceptions, and the issuer’s annual duty to report defaults to the trustee.

nodes.title: Legal Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The text explains legal defeasance, which discharges most obligations on all or selected 2002 Indenture debt securities while preserving payment rights, specified administrative duties, trustee rights and duties, and discharge provisions. Covenant defeasance releases series-specific covenants except payment obligations, so breaches no longer constitute defaults. Either option requires an irrevocable, sufficient trust deposit of cash, government securities, or both; a tax opinion (with an IRS ruling or later law change required for legal defeasance); no existing default, subject to exceptions; and a bankruptcy-related opinion addressing estate and automatic-stay protection, or a first-priority trustee lien for covenant defeasance.

nodes.title: Satisfaction and Discharge
nodes.summary: At the issuer’s request and expense, the 2002 Indenture may be discharged, except for specified transfer or exchange rights, once securities are canceled or all uncanceled securities are due, due within 60 days, or redeemable within 60 days under trustee-approved notice arrangements. The issuer must irrevocably deposit sufficient U.S. dollars, government securities, or both to pay principal, premium, and interest; pay all other amounts due under the indenture; have no existing default or event of default; and provide the trustee an officers’ certificate and counsel’s opinion confirming all conditions are met. The trustee then executes discharge documents.

nodes.title: Modification of the 2002 Indenture
nodes.summary: The 2002 Indenture generally permits changes affecting a series’ holders’ rights with approval from holders of a majority in principal amount of each affected series. Each affected holder’s consent is required for changes to payment maturity or terms, interest calculation or currency, enforcement rights, or the required amendment threshold. Without holder consent, the company and trustee may supplement the indenture for specified purposes, including corporate succession, adding protective covenants or defaults, correcting defects or ambiguities, adding defaults, making changes that do not affect outstanding securities, providing coupon-form securities and exchanges, establishing new series and their terms, and appointing successor or additional trustees.

nodes.title: Amalgamation, Consolidation, Merger or Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The 2002 Indenture permits the company, without debt-security holders’ consent, to merge, consolidate, amalgamate, or transfer substantially all its assets if the successor assumes the company’s obligations, is organized under U.S. law, no default is continuing after the transaction, and other indenture conditions are met. A qualifying transaction is not a default or event of default and does not trigger the related remedies for holders or the trustee.

nodes.title: No Limitations on Additional Debt and Liens
nodes.summary: The 2002 Indenture has no restrictions on additional debt, sale-leasebacks, or liens. The 1991 Indenture, governed by New York law, permits unlimited debt securities in series and issuance without holder consent of equivalent additional securities consolidated into an existing series. Its covenant generally requires the company and subsidiaries to secure debt backed by liens on Operating Property or subsidiary shares or debt equally and ratably with the notes, subject to exceptions including qualifying mortgages for property acquired, constructed, or improved after January 31, 1991, and mortgages existing when property is acquired.

The section describes the 2002 Indenture’s debt issuance and conversion or exchange terms; series-specific events of default, acceleration, waivers, trustee duties, enforcement, and reporting; legal and covenant defeasance; and conditions for satisfaction and discharge. It also sets conditions for mergers and asset transfers and notes there are no restrictions on additional debt, liens, or sale-leasebacks under the 2002 Indenture, contrasting this with the 1991 Indenture’s lien covenant and exceptions.

Its covenants restrict secured borrowing and operating-property sale-leasebacks, subject to listed exceptions, a 10%-of-net-tangible-assets or 15%-of-capitalization threshold, and specified proceeds uses. It also permits mergers or substantially-all-asset transfers to a U.S. successor that is not in default and assumes the issuer’s obligations.

nodes.title: Events of Default, Notice and Waiver
nodes.summary: The 1991 Indenture’s default events include failures to pay principal or premium at maturity or interest for 30 days; covenant breaches uncured for 60 days after notice; certain other-debt defaults or accelerations not cured or annulled within 10 days of written notice; bankruptcy, insolvency, or reorganization events; and series-specific defaults. While a default continues, the trustee or holders of 25% of a series may accelerate its debt, subject to possible annulment. A majority may waive defaults except uncured payment defaults. The issuer must annually certify whether defaults exist; the trustee must notify holders of known uncured defaults within 90 days, but may withhold certain notices in good faith when doing so serves holders’ interests. For notice purposes, “default” excludes grace periods. The trustee may require holder indemnification before acting at their request, and a series majority may direct remedies, subject to legal, liability, and good-faith limits.

nodes.title: Modification of the 1991 Indenture
nodes.summary: The 1991 Indenture may generally be amended with trustee and issuer approval and consent from holders of at least 66⅔% of each affected series. Each affected holder must consent to changes extending maturity or interest-payment dates, reducing interest, principal or redemption premiums, altering accelerated payment on original-issue-discount securities, or impairing payment suits or optional repayment; all affected holders must consent to lowering the amendment threshold. In certain circumstances, a series majority may waive defaults and rescind acceleration. Without holder consent, the issuer and trustee may make amendments concerning corporate succession, added protective covenants and defaults, correcting defects or ambiguities, coupon-form securities and exchange, establishing series terms, and appointing successor or multiple trustees.

nodes.title: Defeasance of Offered Debt Securities in Certain Circumstances
nodes.summary: Under the 1991 Indenture, the board may discharge all obligations on a debt series by resolution and depositing with the trustee money and/or U.S. obligations (or fully U.S.-guaranteed obligations) sufficient to meet all principal and interest payments when due. Discharge is permitted only if an IRS ruling has been received or published confirming it will not create a taxable event for holders.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons

nodes.title: Optional Redemption

Before January 8, 2026, the price is the greater of par or the present value of remaining principal and interest payments, discounted using the applicable Comparable Government Bond Rate plus 15 basis points, with accrued interest added in either case. On or after that date, redemption is at par plus accrued interest. Interest due on or before redemption remains payable to holders of record on the relevant date. Contributions include discretionary Award Contributions, 15% Matching Contributions subject to a maximum dollar limit, Payroll Deductions, and permitted voluntary cash or stock contributions. Cash payroll and voluntary contributions are capped at $125,000 per Plan Year; the Committee sets limits for matches and Outstanding Performance awards. Payroll deductions have minimums of $2 biweekly or $1 weekly, in $0.50 increments, and may be changed or ended by request; they remain effective until changed, ended, or employment terminates. Requests must be in an accepted form, and the Senior Vice President of Total Rewards may prohibit deductions and matching contributions from a final paycheck. Award contributions may be remitted to the account administrator to buy granted shares or delivered directly as stock certificates. Employers remit payroll deductions and matches with participant allocation details; participants remit voluntary contributions, and awards are made as determined by the Committee. Before transfer to the administrator, payroll deductions and matches are employer assets subject to creditor claims in insolvency; they earn no interest, and participants bear stock-value risk.

Employees transferring to a nonparticipating affiliate may keep accounts at Company expense while employed there, but cannot contribute or receive contributions unless eligibility is restored; closure distributions follow the same options and fees. nodes.summary: The Award Program incentivizes exceptional customer service and job performance by Company and Participating Employer Associates, not merely meeting expectations. Its Outstanding Performance component awards Stock for consistently exceptional job-related performance over a month, quarter, or year, via share certificates or shares purchased for the Participant’s Account at the Committee’s discretion. Awards require Committee or delegate approval under established procedures and are subject to individual dollar limits. The Former Great Job component ended in 2007, and all outstanding buttons were canceled September 1, 2008.

Subject to the Plan, the Committee has sole, final discretion to determine Contribution recipients, types, amounts, terms, eligibility, limits, and satisfaction of conditions; designate or terminate Participating Employers and set non-U.S. Associate eligibility; interpret and administer the Plan; adopt, amend, suspend, waive, or rescind rules; appoint agents; correct defects, omissions, or inconsistencies; and make other necessary decisions. Its actions bind all affected persons, subject to later modification. The Committee sets the timing of determinations not specified in the Plan, may modify them, and its listed powers do not limit its broader authority.

Awards, contributions, and stock deliveries must comply with applicable laws and required governmental or exchange approvals; benefits or shares need not be delivered if doing so would violate law or regulation.

nodes.title: 9.4 Securities Law Compliance.
nodes.summary: The Committee may impose securities-law and exchange-related restrictions on contributions, stock purchases, holdings, transfers, and resales, including legends, stop-transfer orders, participant representations, and satisfactory legal opinions. It may delay benefit vesting or delivery, suspend purchases or participation to maintain compliance, and the Company must make reasonable efforts to resume them promptly. Participants have no stockholder rights until shares are credited or delivered, except for previously owned voluntary contributions. Matching and award contributions do not count toward compensation or benefits unless governing plans or agreements provide otherwise. The Plan does not limit other compensation arrangements; it follows military-service law, sets rules for interpreting “or,” number, and gender, and makes headings subordinate to the text.

nodes.title: Plan Administration and Participant Rights
nodes.summary: The Committee may delay benefit vesting or delivery and suspend stock purchases to address securities-law or exchange-rule compliance, while the Company works toward prompt compliance and may suspend participation or purchases as needed. Participants gain stockholder rights only when shares are credited or delivered. Matching and award contributions are special incentive payments excluded from benefit or compensation calculations unless plans or agreements provide otherwise. The Plan does not limit other compensation arrangements. Military-service administration follows applicable federal law; construction rules address word usage, and headings are for convenience, with Plan text controlling.

nodes.title: Plan Approval, Taxes, Employment Rights, and Governing Law
nodes.summary: Contributions made before stockholder approval of the amended Plan are conditional on approval. Payroll Deduction, Matching, and Award Contributions are subject to applicable income-tax withholding and reported as wages; withholding may exceed the authorized deduction to cover taxes. Share distributions or cash for fractional shares are generally not taxable unless law provides otherwise. The Plan does not alter the Company’s rights concerning Associates, including discharge or compensation changes. Delaware law governs, subject to federal securities law and the Company’s Account Administrator agreement.

nodes.title: 9.15 Adjustments upon Changes in Capitalization or Merger.

title: WALMART INC.
summary: The text presents Walmart Inc.’s Director Compensation Deferral Plan, amended and restated effective June 4, 2010, and renamed February 1, 2018. Its contents cover the plan’s purpose, history and effective dates; definitions; director deferral elections; share and cash accounts and interest; payment forms, timing, amounts, death and gross misconduct; administration and appeals; and miscellaneous provisions addressing amendment or termination, non-alienability, taxes, successors, and governing law. It then begins section 1.1, Purpose of Plan.

title: ARTICLE I GENERAL
summary: The Plan originally set director fee amounts and forms, enabled equity participation, and allowed fee deferrals; since June 4, 2010, it serves only to defer fees awarded under the Stock Incentive Plan or otherwise. It recounts adoption and amendment history, a 1,000,000-share authorization subject to adjustment, and the end of new fees and share awards under this Plan from that date. The Committee established 409A-compliant deferral procedures and renamed the Plan in 2010 and 2018. Terms generally cover deferrals from 2005 onward; pre-2005 deferrals remain subject to Appendix A, which is protected from material modification. Distributed shares are charged to the plan under which awarded, with Stock Incentive Plan shares covering any shortfall. The Plan is unfunded: ledger accounts are only payment promises, and Walmart’s obligations are unsecured general contractual obligations.

title: ARTICLE II DEFINITIONS
summary: Defines the plan’s key terms, including affiliates, directors, accounts, fees, stock, valuation, misconduct, interest, service separation, and plan administration. Sets annual deferral-election rules: directors may defer all or part of fees into share or cash accounts, subject to advance filing deadlines and special rules for new or returning directors. Elections are irrevocable after deadlines, apply only to the specified year, and default to no deferral; prorating applies to certain partial-year service and fees.

title: ARTICLE IV DEFERRAL ACCOUNTS
summary: The provisions explain how deferred fees are credited: share accounts receive units based on fair market value, adjusted for stock splits and credited with dividend equivalents, without shareholder or voting rights; cash accounts receive deferred amounts plus daily simple interest through the month before distribution. Directors elect lump-sum or up-to-10-year installment payments, with specified default and legacy elections and restrictions on changing elections. Payments are generally made within 90 days of the distribution date, subject to legal-compliance delays and Code Section 409A. Lump sums and installments specify treatment of cash, shares, fractional shares, and interest. Directors may designate beneficiaries; unpaid benefits are paid in a lump sum after death, or to the estate if no beneficiary applies. For fees paid or deferred on or after April 1, 2006, gross misconduct can trigger repayment, recalculation of deferred balances, interest, offsets, and appeal rights; misconduct affecting fees under other plans is governed by those plans.

title: ARTICLE VI ADMINISTRATION
summary: The Committee administers, manages, interprets, and construes the Plan, with discretion to determine benefit eligibility and amounts and resolve disputes concerning Directors’ or beneficiaries’ rights. It may adopt, change, or repeal administrative rules and practices, and appoint assistants for day-to-day administration. Its decisions are final and binding on Walmart, Directors, beneficiaries, and affected persons, subject to Article VII’s claims procedure. A Committee member may not participate or vote on matters solely concerning that member’s own Plan rights or benefits.

title: ARTICLE VII CLAIMS PROCEDURE
summary: The claims procedure allows a Director or beneficiary to file a written benefit claim with the Committee within one year of the Director’s Distribution Date; late claims eliminate any obligation by the Plan or Walmart and all further Plan rights. Denials must be communicated within 60 days and explain the reasons, relevant Plan provisions, information needed to perfect the claim, and review procedure. Claimants may appeal in writing within 60 days, inspect pertinent documents, and submit written comments. Review decisions are due within 60 days, or within 120 days if special circumstances require an extension, and must state reasons and relevant Plan provisions. Days include weekends and holidays.

title: ARTICLE VIII MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS
summary: The Board or Committee may amend or terminate the Plan, but cannot impair accrued payment or account rights or accelerate deferred-fee payments except as permitted by Code Section 409A. Directors cannot transfer, encumber, or lose account interests to creditors or involuntary proceedings; a qualifying domestic relations order may require a single lump-sum distribution. Walmart withholds legally required taxes, while Directors or beneficiaries bear all related income and excise taxes. The Plan binds Walmart, successors and assigns, Directors, beneficiaries, heirs, and legal representatives. Arkansas law governs, except Delaware law governs Walmart’s internal affairs.

It defines key terms and sets quarterly retainers, election deadlines and defaults, share/unit valuation and dividend adjustments, account credits, conversions, and post-service lump-sum or up-to-10-year installment distributions. nodes.summary: Walmart’s March 2025 policy prohibits officers, employees, directors, their household members, dependents, and controlled entities from trading on material nonpublic information or tipping it, covering Walmart stock and derivatives, other companies’ securities, and certain retirement and stock-purchase transactions. It defines material and nonpublic information, gives examples, and generally allows one trading day after public release for market absorption. It describes severe legal and company disciplinary consequences; requires confidentiality and applies even when trades are independently motivated or after service ends. nodes.summary: Trading-window rules apply to all Directors and specified Associates: officers, participants in Global Leadership Meetings, and those with access to designated or other sensitive financial reports. Eligible personnel may trade from the day after quarterly earnings are released through the next-to-last day of the quarter’s second month, only if they possess no material nonpublic information; trading is generally prohibited otherwise, including certain 401(k), profit-sharing, and stock-purchase-plan transactions. Additional restrictions or corporate-secretary notices may apply; seek guidance if uncertain. Rule 10b5-1 plans may operate outside windows if adopted during an open window without material nonpublic information, meet SEC requirements, and receive advance approval. Plans require good faith, predetermined terms or independent discretion, limits on amendments and simultaneous plans, and submission for approval at least five business days beforehand with required representations. Cooling-off periods are at least the later of 90 days after adoption or two business days after the relevant 10-Q/10-K filing for Directors and Section 16 Officers, and 30 days for other Associates; plan trades then need no further preapproval. Directors and Section 16 Officers must also report adoption, amendment, or termination of certain other preset plans.

B. Hedging of Walmart Stock Prohibited
nodes.summary: Walmart prohibits Associates and Directors, directly or through designees, from hedging or speculating in Walmart Stock because these activities can reduce ownership risks, create conflicts of interest, and misalign their interests with shareholders. Hedging includes transactions designed to offset declines in equity value, such as swaps, collars, short sales, prepaid forwards, futures, and exchange-fund interests; a designee is someone arranged to hedge on their behalf. The ban applies to compensation-related and all other directly or indirectly held Walmart Stock. Speculative derivatives tied to Walmart Stock and transactions that pit personal financial interests against Walmart’s are also prohibited, including short selling. Walmart may impose disciplinary or other action for violations or conduct it considers unethical or improper.

nodes.title: IV. Pre-Clearance Requirements for Directors, Section 16 Officers, and Senior Executives
nodes.summary: Section 16 officers, directors, and officers at Executive Vice President level or higher must obtain pre-clearance at least two business days before any Walmart Securities transaction, including gifts and Trading Plan entries or amendments, by contacting the specified Corporate Secretary office. Approval is discretionary and may involve consultation with management or counsel. If denied, they must not trade or disclose the restriction. Approval does not override bans on trading while holding material non-public information or during closed windows or event-specific restrictions, and expires after two business days.
